<FromTheBinary topic="crud" />

This page shows the patterns for working with entities through the REST API.
The examples assume a local cyoda-go instance on the default port, `8080`. In
mock IAM mode the bearer token is not needed. In JWT mode every request
carries a token; see
[authenticating applications](/build/authenticating-applications/).

The complete endpoint catalogue — parameters, response shapes, error codes —
lives in the [API reference](/reference/api/). Keep that open as you work.

## The shape of the API

cyoda-go speaks REST for CRUD, search, and workflow invocation, and gRPC for
compute nodes. This page covers REST; see
[Build → client compute nodes](/build/client-compute-nodes/) for gRPC and the
[APIs and surfaces](/concepts/apis-and-surfaces/) overview for the decision
framework.

For durable inbound payloads that are not yet entities — a staging buffer at the platform edge — see [edge messages](/build/edge-messages/).

## Create

An entity is created against a registered model in the `LOCKED` state.
Register the model from sample data and lock it first; see
[modeling entities](/build/modeling-entities/). A create against an unknown
model is `404 MODEL_NOT_FOUND`, and against a model that is not locked it is
`409 MODEL_NOT_LOCKED`. A create never discovers or changes the schema on its
own; on a locked model only its
[change level](/build/modeling-entities/#the-change-level-ladder) lets a write
extend it.

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/entity/JSON/orders/1 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "orderId": "ORD-42",
    "customerId": "CUST-7",
    "amount": 120.00,
    "currency": "EUR",
    "lines": [
      { "sku": "AX-1", "qty": 2, "price": 60.00 }
    ]
  }'
```

The path is `/api/entity/{format}/{entityName}/{modelVersion}` — here `JSON`,
`orders`, and version `1`. The response is an array with one element per
committed transaction:

```json
[
  {
    "entityIds": [
      "7ae965b8-e6c1-11f1-9408-ae468cd3ed16"
    ],
    "transactionId": "7ae9652c-e6c1-11f1-9408-ae468cd3ed16"
  }
]
```

`entityIds[0]` on the first element is the **system-assigned UUID** of the
new entity. Capture it — reads, updates, and transitions address the entity
by that UUID, not by the business key `orderId`. The response does not carry
the entity's state; read the entity for that.

The entity's data is a JSON object. A body that is `null`, a number, a
string or a boolean is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` (`expected object, got …`). A JSON array body creates one entity per
element, in transactional chunks of up to `transactionWindow` entities
(default `100`). To create entities of several models in one request, post a
collection to `POST /api/entity/JSON`, where each item's `payload` is the
entity encoded as a JSON **string**.

The server dates the entity at the commit of its transaction. See
[revisions are dated at commit](/build/consistent-reads/#revisions-are-dated-at-commit).

## Read

Fetch the current revision by id:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/api/entity/${ENTITY_ID} \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "amount": 120.00,
    "currency": "EUR",
    "customerId": "CUST-7",
    "lines": [
      { "price": 60.00, "qty": 2, "sku": "AX-1" }
    ],
    "orderId": "ORD-42"
  },
  "meta": {
    "creationDate": "2026-11-22T22:10:09.039097Z",
    "id": "7ae965b8-e6c1-11f1-9408-ae468cd3ed16",
    "lastUpdateTime": "2026-11-22T22:10:09.039097Z",
    "modelKey": { "name": "orders", "version": 1 },
    "state": "draft",
    "transactionId": "7ae9652c-e6c1-11f1-9408-ae468cd3ed16",
    "transitionForLatestSave": "loopback"
  },
  "type": "ENTITY"
}
```

`meta.transactionId` identifies the revision you read. Send it as `If-Match`
on a later update; see [concurrency](#concurrency).

The single-entity read also takes `pointInTime` (the entity as at an instant)
or `transactionId` (the version a committed transaction wrote), but not both.
See [consistent reads](/build/consistent-reads/).

### List a model

List the entities of a model with `GET /api/entity/{entityName}/{modelVersion}`:

```
GET /api/entity/orders/1?pageSize=100&pageNumber=0
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pageSize` | `20` | Entities per page |
| `pageNumber` | `0` | Zero-based page index |
| `pointInTime` | — | Read the model as at this instant |

The order is stable and deterministic. Pages read without `pointInTime` are
read at different moments, so writes between two requests can shift the
pages. For consistent pages, pass one consistency time as `pointInTime` on
every page; see
[consistent paging](/build/consistent-reads/#consistent-paging).

The list endpoint does not accept field filters. For filtered reads —
predicates, result caps, sorting — see
[searching entities](/build/searching-entities/).

## Update

Direct updates use `PUT /api/entity/{format}/{entityId}` (loopback update — stores a new revision without a named transition) or `PUT /api/entity/{format}/{entityId}/{transition}` (update with a named transition). `PUT` has **wholesale-replace** semantics: any field you omit from the body is destroyed. To change only some fields, use [`PATCH`](#partial-update-patch) instead.

The body of a `PUT` is required. An empty body is `400 BAD_REQUEST`, and
nothing is committed.

**Mutations that move the entity between lifecycle states should go through a
named transition**, not a bare loopback update. A named transition is
recorded in the audit trail and runs its processors. The request carries the
complete new entity:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/entity/JSON/${ENTITY_ID}/submit \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "If-Match: ${LAST_TRANSACTION_ID}" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "orderId": "ORD-42",
    "customerId": "CUST-7",
    "amount": 130.00,
    "currency": "EUR",
    "lines": [
      { "sku": "AX-1", "qty": 2, "price": 65.00 }
    ]
  }'
```

The entity's state comes from the workflow, not from the data. Do not model
it as a field in the payload.

To fire a transition **without changing the data**, send the empty merge
patch `{}` with `PATCH` to the transition route:

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/entity/JSON/${ENTITY_ID}/submit \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json' \
  -H "If-Match: ${LAST_TRANSACTION_ID}" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{}'
```

A client can name any transition of the entity's current state that is not
`disabled` and has no `schedule`, whether its `manual` is `true` or `false`.
`GET /api/entity/{entityId}/transitions` lists them. See
[Build → workflows and processors](/build/workflows-and-processors/) for
how to declare transitions.

### Partial update (PATCH)

When you want to change only the fields that moved — without resending (and risking clobbering) the rest of the entity — use `PATCH`:

```http
PATCH /api/entity/{format}/{entityId}
PATCH /api/entity/{format}/{entityId}/{transition}
```

The body is a sparse JSON object applied to the **stored** entity with RFC 7386 (`application/merge-patch+json`) semantics: a non-null key overwrites, an explicit `null` deletes that key, an omitted key is left untouched, and an array is replaced whole.

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/entity/JSON/${ENTITY_ID} \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json' \
  -H "If-Match: ${LAST_TRANSACTION_ID}" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{ "amount": 130.00, "note": null }'
```

The merged result is validated strictly against the model schema — a `PATCH`
never extends the model, even under a change level that permits it. To add a
new field, use `PUT`. On the named-transition route the merge is applied
first, and the transition's processors then run on the merged entity and may
overwrite patched fields. The request is JSON-only (XML ⇒ `415`); RFC 6902
JSON Patch (`application/json-patch+json`) is recognised but returns `501`.

### Concurrency

Every write runs under snapshot isolation with first-committer-wins
validation. A concurrent commit that changes an entity your transaction read
aborts your transaction at commit with a **retryable `409 CONFLICT`**. A
write race lost inside a transaction answers the same `409`, whatever the
transaction did after it. Retry the request.

`If-Match` adds a precondition across requests. It carries the
`meta.transactionId` from your last read, unquoted, and it states the
revision the update starts from:

| `If-Match` | `PUT` | `PATCH` |
|---|---|---|
| A transaction id | Applied only if the entity is still at that revision; otherwise `412 ENTITY_MODIFIED` | Same |
| `*` | Not accepted; answered `412 ENTITY_MODIFIED` | Unconditional; merges onto the current state |
| Absent or empty | Unconditional replace | `428 PRECONDITION_REQUIRED` |

The server checks `If-Match` **once**, when the update starts. Writes that
the update's own transaction makes to the entity afterwards — the engine's
save before a processor's callout, or the commit of a
`COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` segment — do not fail it. A change committed by
another transaction after that check is the retryable `409 CONFLICT`, not
`412`.

On a `412`, read the entity again, reapply your change to the new revision,
and send the new `meta.transactionId`.

## Bounding a write

Every entity write accepts `transactionTimeoutMillis`. It bounds the time that
the server spends before the **first commit**:

```
POST /api/entity/JSON/orders/1?transactionTimeoutMillis=10000
```

When the time elapses, the server rolls the transaction back and fails the
request with `408 TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT`. It commits nothing. If you omit the
parameter, the write has no server-side timeout.

A chunked write is an array body that `transactionWindow` splits into chunks.
The parameter covers the first chunk only. If the time elapses after that, the
server reports a `TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT` element in the per-chunk response
instead of an HTTP `408`.

The server rejects the parameter with `400` on a request that
[joins an open transaction](/build/client-compute-nodes/#1031-transaction-joined-callbacks).
The same rule applies to `transactionWindow` on a write, to `transactionSize`
on a delete and to `timeoutMillis` on a search.

`503 STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE` reports a problem in the storage layer, and it is
**retryable**. It covers three conditions: the connection pool could not supply
a connection, the database aborted the transaction at its idle ceiling, and the
connection to the database went away.

## When a write is visible

A `2xx` response to a write means that the write is **visible to every later
read on every node**. A caller can write and then read its own data back. Every
storage engine delivers this contract — see
[storage engines](/run/storage-engines/#one-application-contract).

## Request rules

The server reads every request strictly:

- **Body members.** A typed request body spells each member exactly as the
  API declares it, once. A member in another letter case, an undeclared
  member, a member written twice, and anything after the JSON value are
  `400`. The detail names the member and its location as a JSON Pointer, for
  example `invalid JSON at "/0": unknown member name "Payload"`.
- **Entity data is yours.** No member of an entity payload is unknown, and
  `"a"` and `"A"` are two fields. A member written twice in one object is
  still refused.
- **Query parameters.** An operation accepts only the parameters it declares.
  Any other name, including another letter case, is
  `400 BAD_REQUEST: unknown query parameter "…"`, with the name in
  `properties.parameter`. A parameter other than an array may be given once.
- **Date-times.** `pointInTime` is RFC 3339, read strictly; see
  [RFC 3339, strictly](/build/consistent-reads/#rfc-3339-strictly).

A response can carry one or more `Cyoda-Warning` headers: a condition that did
not fail the request, such as an entity run by the default workflow because no
workflow is imported for its model. Each value is percent-encoded UTF-8:

```
Cyoda-Warning: no workflows imported for model %E2%80%94 using default workflow
```

See `cyoda help errors` (WARNINGS) for the encoding and the limits.

## What the platform will not store

A payload can be valid JSON and still be unstorable. The server rejects five
forms at the boundary with `400`, on every storage backend and over both REST
and gRPC:

- **A NUL character** (U+0000) at any position in the payload.
- **Unpaired UTF-16 surrogates and invalid UTF-8.** The server reads the raw
  request bytes for this check. A JSON decoder replaces both forms with U+FFFD,
  which would store a character that you did not send.
- **A name that occurs more than once in the same object.** Different parts of
  the system read a different occurrence, so the payload has no single meaning.
- **Content after the JSON value**, such as `{"x":1}}}`.
- **A number outside the `numeric` range of PostgreSQL.**

## Delete

Delete a single entity by id, or delete a matched subset of a model with a condition:

```bash
# Delete a single entity by id
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/entity/${ENTITY_ID} \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

`DELETE /api/entity/{entityId}` removes exactly the entity with that UUID and
returns its id, model key, and the transaction id of the delete. It takes no
query parameters; `pointInTime` there is
`400 BAD_REQUEST: unknown query parameter "pointInTime"`.

```bash
# Delete the entities that match a condition
curl -X DELETE 'http://localhost:8080/api/entity/orders/1?verbose=true' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "type": "simple",
    "jsonPath": "$.status",
    "operatorType": "EQUALS",
    "value": "cancelled"
  }'
```

```json
{
  "deleteResult": {
    "idToError": {},
    "numberOfEntitites": 3,
    "numberOfEntititesRemoved": 3
  },
  "entityModelClassId": "f3a02baa-f92f-5749-879d-61613b4aa4ba",
  "ids": [
    "f7fd0b32-e6c0-11f1-9406-ae468cd3ed16",
    "f7ff12ce-e6c0-11f1-9406-ae468cd3ed16",
    "f7fb4220-e6c0-11f1-9406-ae468cd3ed16"
  ]
}
```

The body of `DELETE /api/entity/{entityName}/{modelVersion}` is a condition
(`QueryConditionDto`) in the [condition DSL](/build/searching-entities/#the-condition-dsl)
that search uses, up to 10 MiB. Only the matching entities are removed.
`numberOfEntitites` counts the matched entities and `numberOfEntititesRemoved`
the removed ones (the field names are spelt this way in the API).
`verbose=true` lists every id the delete attempted in `ids`.

<Aside type="caution" title="An empty body deletes every entity of the model">

A body that is absent, zero-length, or only JSON white space selects **every**
entity of the model. Any other body must parse as a condition; otherwise the
request is `400 INVALID_CONDITION` and deletes nothing. Send the condition you
intend, and omit the body only when you mean "all".

</Aside>

The condition is checked exactly as a search condition is. A malformed
condition is `400 INVALID_CONDITION`, a path the model does not declare is
`400 INVALID_FIELD_PATH`, and an operator that does not fit the field's type
is `400 CONDITION_TYPE_MISMATCH`. Nothing is deleted in any of these cases.

Without `transactionSize` the delete is **one atomic transaction**. If one
matched entity cannot be deleted, the request fails with that entity's error
and deletes nothing. Two cases do not fail it: an entity selected at a
`pointInTime` that is already gone is reported in `deleteResult.idToError`,
and a lost write race is retried by the server. A race that persists answers a
retryable `409 CONFLICT`.

`pointInTime` selects the entities that existed at that instant, in committed
state, and deletes their current rows. It is fenced by the
[consistency time](/build/consistent-reads/#the-consistency-time).

### Deleting in batches

Add `transactionSize` to remove the selection in independent,
version-guarded batches:

```
DELETE /api/entity/orders/1?transactionSize=500
```

Each batch is atomic. A batch that fails deletes nothing, and its error is
reported in `deleteResult.idToError` for each of its entities. The other
batches still run, and a batch that is already committed stays deleted. An
entity that changed after the server selected it keeps its own entry in
`idToError`. Only a batch that met a write conflict is run again.

Without `pointInTime`, the server selects the matching entities again before
each batch. If entities are created at least as fast as the server removes
them, the selection never becomes empty. In that case the server stops at the
batch cap and fails the request with a retryable
**`409 DELETE_NOT_CONVERGED`**. The batches that are already committed stay
deleted. To make a batched delete terminate, supply `pointInTime`.

The server rejects `transactionSize` with `400` on a request that joins an open
transaction.

## Search

cyoda-go supports two query modes:

- **Direct** (synchronous, bounded-or-fail) — API term `direct`.
  Streams results right away as NDJSON. Good for UI lookups and short
  operations. `limit` caps the *matched set* (default 1000, max 10000) and a
  query matching more than that returns `400 SEARCH_RESULT_LIMIT` rather than a
  truncated page — so `direct` suits queries you know produce a bounded, small
  result set.
- **Async** (background, unbounded, paged) — API term `async`.
  Queued as a job, returns a handle you can poll. Result size is
  unbounded; results are paged. Good for large result sets, periodic
  reports, and exports.

Both accept the same condition grammar over entity fields, metadata, and
workflow state. Pick `direct` by default; switch to `async` when a
query would exceed the `direct` limit, would time out, or would hold
resources you need elsewhere. Ordered top-N over a large model belongs on
`async` too. For predicates, pagination, and worked
examples, see [searching entities](/build/searching-entities/).

## Temporal queries

Every entity's history is queryable. Add `pointInTime` to a read or search to
retrieve the state as at that instant:

```
GET /api/entity/{entityId}?pointInTime=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z
```

The bound is **inclusive** (`<=`) and compared at native precision with no
rounding. The instant must be at or before the consistency time; a later one
is `400 POINT_IN_TIME_AFTER_CONSISTENCY_TIME`. The list read stamps the
instant on each entity as `meta.pointInTime`.

This is the primary way to answer regulatory and audit questions: *what did
this customer's balance look like at quarter close?* For the consistency
time, consistent paging and reads inside a transaction, see
[consistent reads](/build/consistent-reads/).

## Change history

Where `pointInTime` answers *what did this look like then*, the change-history
endpoint answers *who changed it, and when*:

```
GET /api/entity/{entityId}/changes
```

The response lists one entry for each transaction that changed the entity,
newest first. A transaction that wrote the entity several times has one
entry. The history lists committed changes only.

Each entry carries `changeType` (`CREATE`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE`),
`timeOfChange`, and a `user` — the principal the change is **attributed** to.
`transactionId` appears when the entity version is available. An entry also
carries who actually performed the change:

- `attributedKind` — the kind of the attributed `user`: `user`, `service`, or
  `system`.
- `executedBy` — `{id, kind}` for the caller that actually executed the change,
  independent of attribution.

The two differ whenever an action happened *because of* someone but not *as*
them. An on-behalf-of write for a user is attributed to that user and
executed by the on-behalf-of client; a scheduled transition firing hours
later is attributed to whoever armed it. Reading `user` alone cannot tell
these apart — read both when that distinction matters. See
[attribution is not authorization](/concepts/authentication-and-identity/#attribution-is-not-authorization)
for how the platform captures it.

`attributedKind` and `executedBy` are **absent** on a change recorded without
attribution, rather than present and `null`. Treat missing as "not recorded"
rather than as a value.

## From a compute node

When your code is reacting to a transition — running a processor or
evaluating a criterion — talk to the platform over **gRPC**, not REST. The
gRPC path preserves the audit association between the transition and the
compute call, brokers identity, and supports streaming. See
[Build → client compute nodes](/build/client-compute-nodes/) for the
implementation pattern.
